view: A report promises that reciting Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt leaves one in the grave and at Resurrection only as long as an obligatory prayer, followed by entry into Paradise.
The answer addresses both the request for timing and the use of delay to deny the Hour: it will occur, and those who see it will feel their wait lasted only part of a day.
After establishing Resurrection and describing its general, moral, and punitive states, including the Great Calamity, the passage turns to the question of when it will happen.
The sūrah establishes resurrection, gathering, and humanity's final fate after the preceding sūrahs' exposition; its oaths mark the subject's decisive climax.
The title al-Nāziʿāt points to angels extracting souls and then to Pharaoh and Moses; the names al-Sāhirah and al-Ṭāmmah also suit the oaths and the sūrah's progression.
The imperfect verb presents the question as recurring: the questioners repeatedly demanded a date after hearing about Resurrection.
The questioners are Quraysh or other disbelieving polytheists, who repeatedly asked the Prophet about the Hour after he warned them of it.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies them with the earlier questioners who asked whether they would be restored to their former state (79:10).

view: A report attributes the verse's revelation to Meccan polytheists mockingly asking the Prophet when the Hour would come.
note: Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes the Ibn ʿAbbās report's chain as weak.

view: Reports from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb and ʿĀʾishah say the Prophet frequently mentioned the Hour and was asked about it until this passage was revealed; ʿĀʾishah says he then stopped.
A report says the Prophet answered Bedouins' question by pointing to the youngest among them and saying their Hour would come if he lived a century.
note: Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the report as unsuitable date-setting because revelation repeatedly says only God knows the Hour.

view: They ask mockingly or sarcastically about the Hour's time, rather than seeking information; the frightening descriptions themselves become material for their taunt.
note: The attribution to Makkan idolaters is reported in some sources; the occasion reports are recorded separately.

view: They impatiently demand that the Hour come soon, deeming it impossible because it has not yet occurred.
note: Rāzī cites 42:18 and Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 10:48 for demands that it be hastened.

view: The sarcastic question is meant to make the questioners' followers think Resurrection has no basis.
The questioners aim to put the Prophet in difficulty by demanding a date he cannot give.
They take the Hour's delay as disproof, assuming an angry God would retaliate immediately as an impetuous human would; the Qur'an rejects that analogy.
The Prophet wished he could answer their timing question, hoping an answer would help them believe.
One reading asks why the Prophet is occupied with mentioning and disclosing the Hour's appointed time.
note: Rāzī pairs this reading with ʿĀʾishah's report that the Prophet kept mentioning and being asked about the Hour until this verse came down.

view: Another reading rebukes the timing question itself: the signs of the Hour's nearness are enough to prepare people, while its time belongs to God alone.
note: This differs from the reading that questions the Prophet's occupation with its appointed time.

view: In ordinary Arabic sāʿah can mean a portion of time, and the definite form can mean the present moment; later it came to mean a conventional sixty minutes and to name a timekeeping instrument.
An indefinite sāʿah in the Qur'an denotes a short, unspecified span, while the definite Hour consistently denotes the decisive event of the Afterlife.
The Qur'an's verbs of coming and rising present the Hour as active and momentous, marking a change in cosmic order.
Naming the event ‘the Hour’ instead of repeating ‘the Great Calamity’ gives the sentence independent force and varies the naming.
A Prophetic report says the Hour will occur only with an anger that God becomes angry.
Signs of the Hour precede its occurrence.
note: Rāzī says the final messenger has given signs of its nearness.

view: Ayyān means ‘when’ and asks about the time of a future event, as distinct from ayn, which asks about place.
Because a time cannot directly predicate an event, the clause is understood as ‘at what time is its appointed establishment?’
Asking for a specific time suggests that the Hour is remote or even impossible.
A question about when seems mismatched with marsā as a place of settlement; a metaphor treats the distant day like a traveler reaching a destination.
Al-Aʿraj reads إيان with kasra on its initial alif.
When Gabriel asked when the Hour would come, the Prophet replied that the one asked knew no more than the asker.
The Qummī commentary glosses the question as ‘when does it come?’ and says its knowledge belongs to God.
The question asks when the Hour or Resurrection will occur, appear, and be established.
note: Some gloss establishment as God's setting the Hour in place; al-Qurtubi says the explanations are close in meaning.

view: Only God knows the Hour's appointed time; it lies beyond the Prophet and all creation, so the timing question receives no date.
The Prophet's responsibility is to warn, giving receptive people a chance to prepare; the questioners' demand for a date should not trouble him.
note: Rāzī adds that the final messenger has already given signs of the Hour's nearness, which suffice for preparation.

view: The question and its explanation connect to the earlier treatment of the Hour in al-Aʿrāf 7:187.
note: Al-Qurṭubī says the different glosses of mursāhā are close in meaning.

view: Knowledge of the Hour ends with God; knowing it requires the annihilation of one's knowledge in divine knowledge and one's self in God's Self.
Marsā evokes a ship coming to rest at anchor: the Hour's irsāʾ is its arrival, establishment, and becoming manifest or fixed. Al-Farrāʾ compares this establishment to justice or truth standing.
Marsā can mean the Hour's endpoint or resting place, like the place where a ship finishes its course and anchors.
note: This is given as an alternative to establishment or occurrence.

view: Marsā can be a verbal noun for anchoring or causing something to rest, or a noun of its time or place; one gloss makes it a time noun from rasa, ‘becoming firm.’
note: Al-Ālūsī compares firmness to firmly rooted mountains.

view: The nautical image of the Hour berthing can suggest that it is near.
